title: The phone on the table
hook: a study found a phone's mere presence reduced working memory, though later studies are mixed (Ward et al.)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the attentional blink: right after catching one thing, the mind can miss the next, and retreat meditators blinked less by grabbing less. Your line was fewer blinks.

Dinner with a friend. Two plates, two glasses, and a phone lying face down by the bread, silent. Nobody touches it the whole meal. It doesn't buzz once. So it isn't doing anything, right? A team of researchers wondered whether that was true. Not a phone that rings or lights up. A phone that does nothing at all, except be there.
screen: `FACE DOWN BY THE BREAD.` → `IT NEVER BUZZES.` → `IS IT DOING NOTHING?`

segments.voice: Adrian Ward and his colleagues gave people demanding tasks that use working memory, the mind's small scratchpad for holding things while you think. Some people left their phones face down on the desk, silenced. Some put them in a pocket or a bag. Some left them in another room. Those whose phones were in another room did best; those with the phone on the desk did worst. And the strange part: people said the phone wasn't on their mind. The researchers' idea was that some attention goes into not checking it, a quiet, steady effort to ignore something that matters to us, and that effort uses some of the same limited capacity these past days have explored. They called their paper Brain Drain. Now the honest part, and it matters. Later studies have been mixed. Some found a similar effect; others tried and didn't. So this is not settled science, and anyone who says a phone on the table definitely makes you less smart is saying more than the evidence does. But look at what the idea asks us to notice. Attention is limited. Wandering costs. Holding on to the first thing makes us miss the next. A silent phone may be one more pull on that limited supply. And the fix the study points to costs nothing. Not willpower. Not a new app. Just distance. Another room.
screen: `FACE DOWN, POCKET, OR ANOTHER ROOM.` · `ANOTHER ROOM DID BEST.` · `LATER STUDIES ARE MIXED.` · `THE FIX IS DISTANCE.`

segments.voice: If you're listening on your phone, finish the lesson first; if not, carry it out of the room now, set it down, and come back. Sit and breathe, and notice whether some part of you is still listening for it, and whether anything in the room gets a little quieter, or doesn't.
The phone on the table. The idea, from one study with mixed follow-ups, that a silent phone in view may quietly draw on attention. Today's word.
screen: `THE PHONE ON THE TABLE — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: another room. The fix costs nothing: not willpower, not an app, just distance. Day twelve seventy-one.

howItsDone: Researchers test the mere-presence effect by placing participants' phones on the desk, in a pocket or bag, or in another room, then comparing scores on working memory tasks; results across later studies have been mixed.
